questions.problem: Consider the vector $u=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ \sqrt{k} \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Given that $u\cdot v=-20$ and $‖v‖=5$,  what is the smallest possible value of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

$$
|u\cdot v|\le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖.
$$

We are given all the quantities in the inequality above, except for $‖u‖.$ So first, we compute $‖u‖$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖u‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(\sqrt{k})^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{14+k}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |-20| & \le \sqrt{14+k}\cdot (5) \\ 4 & \le \sqrt{14+k} \\ {4}^{2} & \le {(\sqrt{14+k})}^{2} \\ 16 & \le 14+k \\ 2 & \le k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest possible value of $k$ is $2.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the formula

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{w}}{\Vert\mathbf{v}\Vert \, \Vert \mathbf{w}\Vert},
$$

we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{{v}_{1}{w}_{1}+{v}_{2}{w}_{2}+{v}_{3}{w}_{3}+{v}_{4}{w}_{4}}{\sqrt{{v}_{1}^{2}+{v}_{2}^{2}+{v}_{3}^{2}+{v}_{4}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{w}_{1}^{2}+{w}_{2}^{2}+{w}_{3}^{2}+{w}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 2+(-4)\cdot (-2)+(-2)\cdot 2}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{10}{\sqrt{25}\cdot \sqrt{16}} \\  & =\frac{10}{5\cdot 4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta=\arccos \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

Example: 
                    Calculating the Cosine of an Angle
canonical_examples.problem: Let $A(-2, 4, -2, 2)$ and $B(4, 0, -1, -4).$ Find the cosine of the angle $\angle{AOB},$ where $O(0,0,0,0)$ is the origin.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let

$$
\begin{aligned}a=\overset{\to }{OA}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,b=\overset{\to }{OB}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Also, let $\theta = m\angle{AOB}$ be the angle between the vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}.$ Then, we can find $\cos \theta$ using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{‖a‖\,‖b‖} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{1}{b}_{1}+{a}_{2}{b}_{2}+{a}_{3}{b}_{3}+{a}_{4}{b}_{4}}{\sqrt{{a}_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}+{a}_{4}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{b}_{1}^{2}+{b}_{2}^{2}+{b}_{3}^{2}+{b}_{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot 4+4\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (-4)}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-4)^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{-14}{\sqrt{28}\cdot \sqrt{33}} \\  & =\frac{-14}{\sqrt{14}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{33}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{14}}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{33}} \\  & =-\sqrt{\frac{7}{33}}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
The **Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality** (sometimes called the **Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz Inequality**) provides a connection between dot products and norms. It states that for any two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, we have the inequality

$$
\vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.
$$

In other words, the absolute value of the dot product is no more than the product of the norms.

For instance, if ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14156912/assets/6f13203f5c0bc85b3af24b0a276e30044825c0133a6e8b42e6500cb20c0e754c.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14156912/assets/809bfd2b9daeb6f8eee30bbe9ddbfe996326dcf1954cd3f9e09e072e95a16aa3.svg) then 

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |3\cdot 5+(-4)\cdot 12| & \le \sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{12}^{2}} \\ |-33| & \le 5\cdot 13 \\ 33 & \le 65.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** An easy trick to remember the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is to think of the formula for the dot product:

$$
\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta
$$

Because $\vert \cos \theta \vert \leq 1,$ we can see that

$$
\vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.
$$

**Watch out!** The above trick is only a mnemonic trick, *not* an actual proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The formula $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta$ is actually a *consequence* of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, so a proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality cannot use the formula.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
The **Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality** (sometimes called the **Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz Inequality**) provides a connection between dot products and norms. It states that for any two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, we have the inequality

$$
\vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.
$$

In other words, the absolute value of the dot product is no more than the product of the norms.

For instance, if ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14156912/assets/6f13203f5c0bc85b3af24b0a276e30044825c0133a6e8b42e6500cb20c0e754c.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14156912/assets/809bfd2b9daeb6f8eee30bbe9ddbfe996326dcf1954cd3f9e09e072e95a16aa3.svg) then 

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |3\cdot 5+(-4)\cdot 12| & \le \sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{12}^{2}} \\ |-33| & \le 5\cdot 13 \\ 33 & \le 65.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** An easy trick to remember the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is to think of the formula for the dot product:

$$
\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta
$$

Because $\vert \cos \theta \vert \leq 1,$ we can see that

$$
\vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.
$$

**Watch out!** The above trick is only a mnemonic trick, *not* an actual proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The formula $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta$ is actually a *consequence* of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, so a proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality cannot use the formula.

tutorials.name: The Angle Between Two Vectors
tutorials.problem:
Now, using the dot product, we can define the angle $\theta$ between two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $n \ge 2$.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14156912/assets/8244d121c65d655f42378c68e1a197528fb2db60a3890b3842e3c93692d88071.png)

To do that, we say that $\cos\theta$ will be equal to the ratio of the two sides of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, as follows:

$$
\cos\theta	=	\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert}
$$
